lessons.title: The first aider's role and scene safety
lessons.html:
What first aid is

First aid is the immediate help given to an injured or ill person until professional medical help arrives. Its aims are to preserve life, prevent the condition from getting worse and promote recovery. On farms, in abattoirs and in processing plants, help can be far away, so a trained first aider can make the difference between life and death.

Important: this lesson gives background knowledge only. To act as a workplace first aider you must complete hands-on training and assessment with an accredited first aid training provider, and keep your certificate current.

The law

The OHS Act 85 of 1993 and its regulations require employers to provide first aid facilities and trained first aiders in many workplaces. Know who the first aiders are on your site and where the first aid boxes are.

Approach: check for danger first

Never become a second casualty. Before approaching:

  • Look for dangers: moving machinery, electricity, ammonia, traffic, fire, agitated animals, deep water, unstable loads.
  • Make the area safe if you can do so without risk: switch off and isolate machinery, stop traffic, move away from a gas leak.
  • If it is not safe, keep others away and call for specialist help.

Protect yourself from infection

Blood and body fluids can carry infections such as HIV and hepatitis B. Always wear disposable gloves from the first aid kit when there is blood. Use a face shield or pocket mask for rescue breaths if available. Wash your hands afterwards.

Call for help

Shout for help and get someone to call emergency services. In South Africa, call 10177 for ambulance services or 112 from a cellphone, or the private ambulance or site emergency number your workplace uses. Give the exact location (farm name, GPS pin, road and landmarks), what happened, number of casualties and their condition. Send someone to meet the ambulance at the gate.

Recording

After any incident, complete the first aid register and incident report. Record what happened, the injuries seen, the treatment given and where the casualty was referred.

lessons.title: Primary survey and basic life support
lessons.html:
Assessing the casualty: DRSABC

  1. Danger: make sure the scene is safe.
  2. Response: tap the shoulders and shout 'Are you all right?' If there is no response, the person is unresponsive.
  3. Shout for help: get someone to call the ambulance and bring the AED (automated external defibrillator) if the workplace has one.
  4. Airway: open the airway with the head tilt, chin lift.
  5. Breathing: look, listen and feel for normal breathing for no more than 10 seconds. Occasional gasps are not normal breathing.
  6. Circulation / CPR: if not breathing normally, start CPR.

Adult CPR (standard basic life support)

  • Kneel beside the casualty, who must be on their back on a firm surface.
  • Place the heel of one hand in the centre of the chest, other hand on top, arms straight.
  • Push down about 5 to 6 cm at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute, letting the chest come back up fully each time.
  • If trained and willing, give 2 rescue breaths after every 30 compressions. If not trained or unwilling, give continuous chest compressions.
  • As soon as an AED arrives, switch it on and follow its spoken instructions. Make sure nobody touches the casualty during analysis and shock.
  • Continue until professional help takes over, the person starts breathing normally, or you are too exhausted to continue.

Recovery position

If the casualty is unresponsive but breathing normally, place them in the recovery position on their side so the airway stays open and fluids can drain from the mouth. Keep checking breathing. If breathing stops, start CPR.

Choking

If an adult is choking but can cough, encourage coughing. If they cannot cough, speak or breathe, give up to 5 back blows between the shoulder blades, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts. Repeat. If they become unresponsive, start CPR and call for help.

These skills can only be learnt properly by practising on a manikin with an accredited instructor.

lessons.title: Common workplace injuries and conditions
lessons.html:
Managing injuries until help arrives

Severe bleeding

Knife and saw injuries in meat plants can cause serious bleeding. Wearing gloves, apply firm direct pressure on the wound with a sterile dressing or clean pad. Keep pressing. If blood soaks through, add more dressings on top; do not remove the first one. Lay the casualty down and call for help. Watch for shock. Tourniquets should only be used by people trained in their use.

Shock

Shock is a life-threatening drop in blood flow, often from blood loss or burns. Signs include pale, cold, clammy skin, fast weak pulse, fast breathing, confusion and thirst. Lay the casualty down, treat the cause, keep them warm with a blanket, raise the legs if no injury prevents it, and do not give food or drink. Get urgent medical help.

Burns

Cool the burn under cool running water for at least 20 minutes. Remove rings or watches near the area before swelling starts. Cover loosely with cling film or a clean non-fluffy dressing. Never apply butter, toothpaste or ointments, and never burst blisters. For chemical burns, brush off dry chemical and flush with plenty of water, and check the product label or safety data sheet. Seek medical help for serious burns.

Fractures and sprains

Keep the injured part still and supported in the position found. Do not try to straighten it. Support with padding or a sling. For sprains, rest, apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth and raise the limb.

Eye injuries

For chemical splashes, flush the eye with clean running water for a long time, holding the eyelid open, and get medical help. Do not remove objects stuck in the eye.

Other emergencies

  • Electric shock: switch off the power before touching the casualty.
  • Heat exhaustion: move to shade, cool the person and give sips of water if fully conscious.
  • Snakebite: keep the person calm and still, remove tight items, and get to medical help urgently. Do not cut, suck or apply ice.

Key points

  • Always check for danger and protect yourself with gloves.
  • Follow DRSABC and start CPR if the casualty is not breathing normally.
  • Control severe bleeding with firm direct pressure.
  • Cool burns under running water for at least 20 minutes.
  • Record every incident and treatment.
  • Hands-on training by an accredited provider is required to be a first aider.

A casualty is unresponsive but breathing normally. What should you do?
